title: Review: Kinetic theory of gases; Temperature, internal energy, thermal equilibrium; First law of thermodynamics and p–V work; Specific heat capacity and latent heat; Charge and current
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EL01-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; EL01-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; T01-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; T01-1#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EL01-1#N.12, EL01-1#N.11, T01-1#N.5, T02-1#N.10, T02-uk1#N.10b, T06-1#N.8a, T06-uk1#N.8, T07-1#N.10, T07-uk1#N.8, EL01-1#N.6a, T01-1#N.11, T02-1#N.3a. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Current
items.clue: Rate of flow of charge through a cross-section.

items.label: Coulomb
items.clue: Unit: the amount passing a place in a wire when 1 A flows for 1 s.

items.label: Thermal equilibrium
items.clue: Condition of bodies in contact with no net energy transfer between them.

items.label: Temperature
items.clue: Property that decides which way net energy flows between two bodies in contact.

questions.stem: A copper wire has a thick section X joined to a thin section Y, and there is a steady current in the wire. How do the currents I_X and I_Y in the two sections compare?

options.text: They are equal: the same charge passes each cross-section per second.
I_Y is greater, since the charges move faster through the narrow section Y.
I_X is greater, since the thick section X holds more of the charge carriers.
It depends on the direction of the current, as current decreases along a wire.

questions.stem: Several wires meet at a junction in a circuit with steady currents. A student measures a current of 1.20 A in one wire leading into the junction, and currents of 0.70 A and 0.40 A in two wires leading out of it. The ammeters are ideal and read correctly. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The other wires at the junction carry a net current of 0.10 A away from it.
0.10 A of the current was used up as charge passed through the junction.
Charge is building up at the junction at a rate of 0.10 C each second.
An unmeasured wire must carry 2.30 A, the sum of the three measured currents.

questions.stem: Sample P is warmed from 10 °C to 30 °C. Sample Q is warmed from 290 K to 310 K. Which statement about the two temperature changes is correct?

options.text: P's rise of 20 °C is equivalent to a rise of 293 K.
The changes differ, since kelvins and °C differ in size.
Both undergo the same temperature change, 20 K.
P's rise is larger, since P's temperature tripled.

questions.stem: 0.20 kg of water and 0.20 kg of cooking oil, both at 20 °C, are each supplied with 12 kJ of energy. Specific heat capacities: water 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, oil 2000 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Assume no energy is lost. Which statement about their final temperatures is correct?

options.text: The oil ends at 50 °C and the water at about 34 °C.
The water ends at 50 °C and the oil at about 34 °C.
They end at the same temperature, as each gets 12 kJ.
The oil ends at 30 °C and the water at about 14 °C.

questions.stem: A student uses the electrical method to find the specific heat capacity of a brass block. Her value is 10% higher than the data-book value. Which change to her method would most reduce this difference?

options.text: Repeat the experiment three times and calculate a mean value
Use a thermometer with a finer scale, reading to 0.1 °C
Wrap the block in thick insulation and put a lid of insulation on top
Use a lower heater power so the block heats more slowly

questions.explanation: Less energy escapes to the surroundings, so more of VIt raises the block's temperature. The value of c falls towards the true one.

questions.stem: A sealed container of gas is heated from 27 °C to 177 °C. By what factor does the mean kinetic energy of the gas molecules increase?
questions.explanation: T rises from 300 K to 450 K. Mean kinetic energy ∝ T, so it rises by 450/300 = 1.5.

questions.stem: An ideal gas is heated from 27 °C to 927 °C. By what factor does the rms speed of its molecules increase?
questions.explanation: ½m(rms speed)² ∝ T, so rms speed ∝ √T. √(1200/300) = √4 = 2.0.

questions.stem: An ideal gas is in a cylinder whose walls and piston are perfectly insulated. The gas expands, pushing the piston outwards. What happens to the temperature of the gas?

options.text: It stays the same, because no energy is transferred to or from the gas by heating.
It falls, because the gas does work on the piston and no energy enters by heating.
It rises, because the molecules move further apart and gain energy as they spread out.
It stays the same, because the fall in pressure exactly balances the rise in volume.

questions.stem: A heat pump warms a house. Its working gas goes round a cycle. In each cycle, 300 J of work is done on the gas while it is compressed, the gas does 100 J of work while it expands, and it takes in 600 J by heating from the cold air outside. How much energy does it give out by heating to the house in each cycle?
questions.explanation: ΔU = 0 over a cycle, so net Q = net W = 100 − 300 = −200 J. 600 − Q_out = −200, so Q_out = 800 J.

questions.stem: Predict first. A copper wire forms part of a circuit carrying a steady direct current. Which statement about the charge carriers in the wire is correct?

options.text: Free electrons drift slowly towards the positive terminal of the cell.
Electrons travel at close to the speed of light, so a lamp lights at the instant the switch closes.
Protons move along the wire, from the positive terminal towards the negative one.
Electrons leave the cell and some are used up in the lamp, so fewer return to the cell.

questions.explanation: In a metal the charge carriers are free electrons. Being negative, they are attracted towards the positive terminal, and on average they drift only slowly (typically well under 1 mm s⁻¹).

questions.stem: A thermometer at room temperature, 20 °C, is placed in a cup of water at 70 °C. Its reading rises for a while and then stays steady. Why does the steady reading give the temperature of the water?

options.text: All energy transfer between the thermometer and the water has then stopped completely for good.
The thermometer then has as much internal energy as the water in the cup, so the two readings match.
The cold in the thermometer has then all flowed out into the water, so it can read correctly.
They are then in thermal equilibrium, so no net energy is transferred between them.

questions.stem: An electric kettle heats 250 g of water from 18 °C to 90 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. How much energy is transferred to the water? Ignore energy transferred to the kettle and surroundings.
